utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you ever informed by any of your employees that they would be present during searches of the buses?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, you also told us yesterday that you accompanied two convoys. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you stated that the reason was that you wanted to feel how it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, that was only with regard to one of the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to the other, he had a very specific reason that he told us about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you accompanied one of these convoys. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said yesterday that I accompanied them twice. Once to Vlasic and once to Gradiska. So it wasn't once; it was twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I found it. It's page 43. Exactly your words: "Firstly I wanted to experience in person what the ride was like, how the passengers felt on the trip." Mr. Bojinovic, these people were leaving Banja Luka and other municipalities. They lost jobs. They lost accommodation. There was terror around them. They were leaving a place which they knew, and they were leaving for a place which they didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this. This is a comment, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm just going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't agree with you, Mr. Cunningham. Let's hear the question now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: They were -- they didn't know where they will end up. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How do you -- how do you think they might have felt?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you say. What you said just now, that is your view, that people did not know where they would go, that terror reigned, that they had lost their jobs. That is the way you describe all of this, not I. The question is how I think they felt? I would answer this question to you if I were Sigmund Freud or Erich Fromm, if I were a psychiatrist or a psychologist. That is the only way in which I could give a qualified answer. Otherwise I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you do not agree that they were leaving because they were frightened?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely the reason why they were leaving, the fact that they did not feel safe. But all the other qualifications you gave are your qualifications. I'm not denying it; I'm not challenging it. It is certain that people were leaving for reasons of safety. That is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But tell us why it was necessary for you to go on the bus to feel how they felt?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that. It would be illogical for the agency to complete its work without me seeing specifically on the spot what was going on and what things looked like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now move to a subject which you already mentioned, and it is whether the people were frightened or not. Yesterday, you said on page 46, question: "Who was leaving?" You said: "Whoever felt that it was safer for them to go." Can you describe very briefly the conditions in Banja Luka. Did you learn why these people thought that it was not safe for them to stay in the Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to assume that the question deals with the time period that he was chief of the agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would take that for granted, Mr. Cunningham. Was there conflict in Banja Luka at the time? Was there a war in Banja Luka? Let's start from here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So if there was no conflict, the conflict had not arrived in Banja Luka, why on earth should someone not feel safe living there? And not just one, but so many people, the majority of whom you described as Muslims? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, these people were not from Banja Luka only. It's not exactly the way it was, that Muslims were leaving Banja Luka en masse. We were contacted by people from Banja Luka and from places where conflicts were nearby. But Banja Luka was peaceful. There weren't any conflicts there. Many Muslims remained in Banja Luka, and they still live there. And I see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But also many Muslims left from Banja Luka at the time when you were chief of the agency.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So why would those Muslims who left between July and December when you were chief of the agency, why would these Muslims not feel safe in Banja Luka? What was happening in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. It was peaceful in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, back to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, do you agree with the statement that there were, in fact, very, very long queues in front of your agency? I will read it. I will state it exactly: "The queues were very long. They were there from morning until evening." Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The queues were not long?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges approximately during the time you worked for the agency how many people left on convoys?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say that precisely. But it can be calculated on the basis of the data provided here. Every month about two or three buses left, and if you take into account the fact that there are about 52 to 55 seats on every bus then you'll get the appropriate figure. I'm not a mathematician, so I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it more than 100? Was it more than 500? Was it more than 1.000?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this figure of 100.000 or 500.000, that is not correct. Now, whether it was less than a thousand or more than a thousand, that is possible. But 100.000? 50.000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There may have been a mistake in the interpretation. No one mentioned 100.000 or 500.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My question was, was it more than 100?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One hundred, or 100.000. Could you please be very specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm as specific as possible. I'm talking was it more than 100 people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two buses account for 100 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you are telling the Judges that over these six months you worked for the agency, there were only about 600 people who left?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I object to that. That's not what he's saying. That's a misstatement of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Rephrase your question, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you state that there were approximately 100 people per month leaving, so how many -- okay, I will read it exactly. "Two buses account for 100 people." And on previous occasion, he said that there were two or three buses per month.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And he also said at one time there were six buses that left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that was only once actually what he said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So can you give us, please, an approximate number of people who left through your agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only use the facts that I already told you about. Apart from that, I have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you keep records? Did the agency keep records of the flow of people leaving through the agency, on the agency's buses? I suppose if you sold tickets, you knew exactly how many tickets you sold?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had an accountant? So I suppose at the end of each month you would know exactly whether you had collected enough money to cover the wage bill.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't think he knows that there's a question on the floor, Your Honour. I think he was confused by Ms. Richterova's inadvertent interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put the question. Mr. Bojinovic, a very simple question. You were in charge of this agency. You told us that tickets were sold at the agency. So I suppose that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I did not say that. Tickets were not sold at the agency. Citizens would pay money into the account, the bank account at the post office or at the bank. I kindly ask the Defence to protect me from this kind of thing and this kind of confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham would be very glad to do that. Did you keep accounts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was paying you the fees -- the ticket fees? The bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Money is paid into the bank account of the agency, and then that money can be taken from the bank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you were charging 14.000 dinars per trip?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise for interrupting, that's the October fee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said it was standard. Were you charging 14.000 dinars per trip more or less throughout the period you were responsible for the agency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I headed the agency, the price of the ticket was a standard one. However, in view of the inflation of the dinar vis-a-vis the mark, the figure could vary. So it wasn't 14.000 for each and every journey, for example, because journeys differ. Those to Gradiska from those to Vlasic, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In those months, which was the highest and which was the lowest? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you make an average?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can, I am not opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, you give us an average. If it varied from month to month, taking the aggregate, on an average, which would you suggest? You were the chief, not I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you an exact average. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would 14.000 dinars be a fair guess?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand this guessing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Guessing. Would you consider -- if I told you that on an average each ticket averaged 14.000 dinars, maybe one month it was higher, one month it was lower, on an average during those months, would you accept it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, yesterday and also today you were shown a payroll account. I'm referring to the one in December. Perhaps someone can show the witness DB277, please, once more. You can give him mine if you want. 277. Just make it available. In the meantime, can you dig up, please, 290. That shows the payroll for December. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you assure me that that does not include any payments of arrears of salary not paid in the months before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible, but I cannot give you the exact truth with 100 per cent certainty. Time has gone by, and I cannot remember all of that. It is possible that there were some arrears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you look at DB290, which is also the payroll for July, and then look again at 277, would you agree with me that there were other payrolls for the intervening months, that is, August, September, October, and November, which we don't have here but which would show payment of salaries to you and your staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Every salary was calculated, and it was known exactly what each and every employee's salary was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, did you ever encounter problems during those months, July to December, meeting with your salary bill? Not yours personally, yours and also your staff. Did you always have the money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you left the agency, had you made a profit? Was the agency in the red or had it made a profit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe it just broke even. Perhaps there was some money left, a symbolic sum of money still left in the account. However, I can't say for sure as I was not the head accountant. I believe that by the time the agency ceased to operate, there was very little money left in the account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you add together the payroll total for December and that for July, which amounts to 900-something thousand dinars, and you divide it by 14.000 dinars, it only took 68, make it 69 passengers to cover the entire payroll for those two months. Just 68, 69. And I'm sure there were more than 69 passengers that you escorted out of Banja Luka, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you're asking me is a very complex question. I don't think I can provide an answer. Or at least not an accurate answer, not a truthful answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova, he's back to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, you mentioned yesterday that there were lists of people who were supposed to board the buses, and these lists had to be double-checked. Who double-checked them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station, the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where are the lists now, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also had to keep books, accountants' books and other books of your work. What happened to these documents after you were closed, the agency was closed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The files remained in the same offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was there anyone who was left in the office?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no one to stay. There was nothing for anyone to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So do you tell the Judges you just left everything in the offices and just locked the premises and nothing else happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand the question correctly, you're asking me whether our files or documents were left behind in the offices. Well, those files, those documents stayed at the Security Services Centre. If the agency had any files, they must have stayed there. I'm not sure what became of them really.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So what happened to this account book? Did they stay with the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour. He just said he's not sure what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps you can rephrase the question, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Because it's a little bit confusing, your answer. Because you said those files, those documents stayed at the Security Services Centre. And it's not quite clear what files, what documents you are talking about. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Which documents stayed with the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we misunderstood each other. The Security Services Centre is where persons where checked, whether the persons were suspicious or not, and then the list would go back to us. I'm not sure if they kept anything for themselves. But I assume they must have. The only document that we had at our disposal was the list of people leaving, and this stayed in the agency once the agency had ceased to operate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where are the accountant books now? Do you know? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Just when the agency ceased to operate, the occupational inspector officially shut down the offices. The Bandics took their things away, and the rooms were left empty with papers -- with sheets of paper scattered all over. None of the personnel agency were interested any longer because no one could enter those rooms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did these accountant books stay in the premises, just to make it clear? Or did the accountant take them with him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The accountant did not take those books away. I believe that the offices were later redecorated because the local commune was also there. So my assumption is that all the documents had been thrown away as unimportant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When we had this very first document today, you were appointed by the crisis staff. This was a government agency. Would you agree with me that this was a government agency? Wouldn't it be normal -- To avoid an objection asking two questions, would you agree that it was a government agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the agency of whoever had founded it. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So wouldn't it be normal that you would provide the records to the authority who established this agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you didn't do it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one requested that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how was it that you were closed in December? There were no people wishing to leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. The role of the agency was taken over by the Refugees' Commission. That's after the agency had ceased to operate. For a while, the offices that we had used were closed. Later, this work was continued by the Commission for Refugees. That was no longer my concern, who worked there. I know that they pursued the same kind of activity that we had before them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also told us that, in fact, Banja Luka was a very peaceful town, nothing was really happening. Have you ever heard any comments made by Serb politicians to the effect that only five per cent [Realtime transcript read in error "persons'] of non-Serbs can stay in the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Five persons? Five per cent. If it was translated as five persons --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Have you heard any comment that only 5 per cent at the most --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I just want the time period to be specified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have to be specific on this. During his stay in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During the period July/December.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you're waiting for an answer. I don't think I heard the end of your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. I will repeat my questions. Did you hear any of the Serb politicians, including Radoslav Brdjanin, ever stating only 5 per cent at the most of non-Serbian population can live in this area and they must show their loyalty to this area? Did you hear such a comment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you hear a comment that there are so many nasty people who appeared in the area of Krajina and that we Serbs would cleanse the area of this vermin?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything like that from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you hear during your stay in Banja Luka any negative comments towards non-Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, while you worked at the agency, did you have any dealings with Predrag Radic, the mayor of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were talking about all kinds of municipal regulations which you followed during your work. So are you telling us that you didn't have any contact with municipal officials?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no contact whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it must be followed, my other question, why not? You were working in Banja Luka following municipal regulations. Why didn't you have any contacts with Predrag Radic or other municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can ask the witness whether in his position as head of a government agency he considered himself and his agency accountable to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, if you heard this question by the Judge, would you be so kind and answer it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please specify, substantiate. I would like to have it in a clearer form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were the chief of a government agency. Did you consider yourself accountable to, answerable to anyone? And was your agency accountable, answerable to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one ever made us accountable or requested reports on our monthly work. The agency, however, was indeed accountable to the government bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, you didn't have any dealing with Predrag Radic you already answered. Have you ever heard any comment stating that your agency was extorting money from non-Serbs and that it was what was happening? Isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anyone stating that the agency was extorting money from people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, do you have any explanation why would a Serb stating something like this, that you were extorting money from non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That calls for him to speculate on another person's thought process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyone, not just Serbs. Would anyone, particularly in he or she is a Serb, would anyone would have any justification - now it's no longer a speculation - have any justification in making that accusation to your agency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the question is what I understand it to be, whether a Serb or anyone else ever put forward any such accusations, let me tell you the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Tell me. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just not sure which question to answer now. I'm slightly confused. Can you please specify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll explain to you. You have already answered the big question; namely, whether you are aware anyone made an accusation against your agency that -- in the sense that it was extorting money from non-Serbs. And you answered no, never heard of any such accusation. And my question to you is this: Would anyone have any justification in making such accusation against the agency, especially if that someone happens to be a Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Maybe it would have been with malice that someone might have said something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, did you, again, during the time you were the chief of this agency, did you ever speak to any international organisations?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Journalists came over from other European countries to speak to me. Local journalists also came, domestic journalists, and there is a document about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you speak to any humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Be specific. I mean, you are doing a cross-examination. So you can be more specific than this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while. There's something I must have not --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, do you have an explanation that there should be outsiders who considered your agency as a way how to cleanse non-Serb population from the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the question because it's unclear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I would agree with you that it is not exactly the clearest of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will rephrase it as best I can do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How would you explain -- how would you think that there were outsiders, there were people, who called your agency an agency who participated in cleansing of the area of non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that there were any such people. I said had there been any such people, it would have been out of sheer envy or malice. I never stated that there were any such people, nor that I had heard of them myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we may have a problem of interpretation here because that was never suggested to you. And I think you may not have understood the question at all. So I'll try and intervene, give a hand here. If someone from outside described your agency as an instrument adopted at the time to ethnically cleanse the area from non-Serbs, would you accept that statement as a true criticism of your agency, or not? Does it reflect what you wanted to ask, Madam Richterova? If not, please stop me and rephrase it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If such a criticism was leveled, a criticism saying that the agency was a tool of ethnic cleansing, this would indeed be a misinterpretation. Please allow me to explain. People are leaving an unsafe area. Once the war was over, they came back to their homes. There's no ethnic cleansing there to be spoken of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the only reason why this agency was established was to facilitate the ethnic cleansing of Krajina from non-Serbian population. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you want to tell the Judges and to the Court that there was no ethnic cleansing whatsoever on the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is too general. All I can tell you about is the role of the agency. The agency had the following role: It was a humanitarian role. It was there to assist, to assist whoever was in need, all the people whose lives were at risk. The agency was there to assist them. We helped people. Yet, some have tried to misrepresent this stating that the agency and the Autonomous Region of Krajina were into ethnic cleansing instead. But we must know that the differences and the discrepancy between these two are huge. We were organising safe transfer for people to be taken to safe places. On the one hand you had cases where people from the Federation did not even have an opportunity to do so; but rather, were made to leave their own areas across mountains and through minefields. I think there is an inversion at work here to shift the blame to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Krajina and to the agency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojinovic. I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. So I think we will have -- do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the only thing I wanted to do was to tender the documents I used in my examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the documents are tendered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a short break because we have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just raise then before the break, before the documents are entered into the evidence, I would like to be told the provenance of these documents, where they come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: They come from documents that were supplied by the OTP, I guess. They came off our database.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, two of the documents, some of the documents, but sorry, not the other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, they came off the database. I have no other idea where --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- I hear what Mr. Cunningham says. I want chapter and verse, please, of where these documents come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll take chapter and verse from the Court, not from Ms. Korner. If the Court wants to know, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We obviously want to know. I mean that has been the practice with each and every document that has been forthcoming from whichever, be it the Prosecution or be it the Defence. So if you're not in a position to give us that information yourself today, Mr. Ackerman not being here, I can understand that. But it will need to be resolved when he comes back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the moment I'm objecting to the admission of these documents into evidence. The ones that where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will deal with all this when we reconvene 25 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just apologise. It was my fault Your Honours were kept waiting. I got caught up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We all do that. So no need to apologise. Just happens. I take it there is no re-examination, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are a few questions, Mr. Bojinovic, from the Bench. Judge Janu from the Czech Republic is going to start. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I have just two simple questions for you. Mr. Bojinovic, was it the practice -- am I right, was it the practice that before the people were put on the buses, on the convoy, there was a list of those people, and the list was sent for the checkup, for the confirmation, to some official place - I don't know, security centre, police, or municipality? Am I right in this?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my question is: Did you ever put anybody on the bus who without the documents or without being on the list which was sent to this official place?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And am I right that from the previous question in the cross-examination that you are aware or you know the position of Predrag Radic in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the position that he held, but I did not have the opportunity of speaking to him because he was mayor and he was very busy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Was this position of Mr. Radic in your opinion the high position?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was. It was a responsible position because Banja Luka is a relatively big town. And I think it's a good position, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Bojinovic, if I put to you that Mr. Radic considered your agency, based on any legal ground, and operating against the will of the municipality and against the public interests, what would be your answer or comments?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, Mr. Radic is a person who commands respect. During the war, he was mayor of Banja Luka, and Banja Luka was a peaceful town. So that is the good side of things. Secondly, if he had such an opinion or made such a statement, I respect anybody's statement. That is his statement. I would not exactly agree with it, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Taya.

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Taya comes from Japan. She has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Among the employees of the agency, you were the only person who was appointed by the decision of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: The others, apart from initial employees who were there already 1st July 1992, were hired by you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Then, initial members, the four persons, Perka Bandic, Slobodan Bandic, Stevo Gojanovic, Ljilja Miljkovic, those initial members, how did they become hired?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You have never asked?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You said the agency was a governmental organisation. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. What do you mean by that? You mean the agency was an organisation under the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a bit of a complex matter. The agency was founded at the time when the conflicts started and, well, when times were complicated. It was established by the Krajina. Well, let me say to you that the agency was not part of the Krajina government but it did belong to its founder. So the agency is an organisation of some authorities that existed then. It's not an arbitrary affair; it's not that I founded it, or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: You said it was established by the Krajina. But what does it mean? The ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the crisis staff. I learned about it when I came to Banja Luka. I could not say anything else to you in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: During when you worked as the chief of the agency, you received very minimum salary which was far from maintaining living of your family. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Then how did you make living during that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an extended family living in Glamoc. And I got food from there because this is an area that is well known for its produce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have a very simple question for you. I'm interested in knowing exactly how this agency closed its doors. Who took the decision? How was it communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A representative of the commissioner's office for refugees addressed the agency, and probably the municipal authorities. The municipal authorities, at any rate. And a decision was passed by the work inspectorate of the town of Banja Luka to have the agency closed down. And I don't know what happened next. When I say what happened, I mean the employees who worked in the agency. I know that the Office of the Commissioner for Refugees continued doing a similar kind of work, and then the Ministry for Refugee grew out of that office. It still exists, and it is attached to the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you given a procedure to follow in closing down and winding up the affairs of this agency?

utterances.speaker: MILOS BOJINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Bojinovic, for being kind enough to come here to The Hague, to this Tribunal, to give evidence as a witness called by the Defence and for having answered patiently --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. And I just wish to apologise if I was not unclear at certain points because that was not my wish. It had to do with mistakes in the interpretation. So I'm sorry if I was unclear at certain points. I respect this Honourable Court, which is the normal thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Bojinovic. That's very nice to hear. And I'm sure that you mean what you say. I, on my part, on behalf of the two Judges that sit with me in this case, Judge Janu and Judge Taya, but also on behalf of the Tribunal in general, I would like to once more for having come over. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher out of this courtroom, and you will receive all the assistance you require to enable you to return home at the earliest. And our last words to you, of course, is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I wish you all the best as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So now we have this problem on these documents that you referred to. Do you want to -- do you wish to add anything, Ms. Korner, or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the simple thing is we've done a check and we find no record that these are documents that we gave to the Defence. These wage slips came from the Defence as part of Mr. Ackerman's early disclosure. And we, then, used them in respect of the Witness BT, whatever the number was. So I'm asking at the moment simply that we be told how these documents came into possession of the Defence. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which documents are we referring to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All the DB -- all the DB documents, Your Honour. I know some, I know your legal officer wants to tell us we've exhibited some as Prosecution exhibits, that's right, but those are the same documents that we got through disclosure; they're not our documents as far as we can tell. Certainly, the wage slips which were exhibited when the witness we called gave evidence come from Mr. Ackerman. They have been re-exhibited as DB exhibits, and I'm asking purely and simply where these documents come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I can't answer that question right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we've done as we have done in the past. They are being admitted for the time being with the caveat that the information is still required and the Trial Chamber would then be in a position to confirm the continuation -- continuing presence in the records or expunge them from the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has objected but the objection is on no clear grounds to me. I don't know if it's a foundation objection, or a relevancy objection, or simply we object because we don't know where they come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You have a right to now, but again, you weren't here in the early stages of the trial when we had the same problem in the inverse, the problem is a question of this is one way of establishing authenticity or at least the source -- the attendability of the source.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To be absolutely clear, I'm not objecting obviously on the grounds of relevance. What I'm objecting to is their admission on the basis that we simply do not know from what source the documents come from, and that, therefore, goes to the question of the weight that Your Honours will attach to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: That makes it clear rather than a simple objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. And this is something that I'm sure Mr. Ackerman will be able to enlighten us upon. Any further -- yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, when I did my cross-examination, I was using two documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you had two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: One was tendered into exhibit under P2708. And the other one I forgot to tender, so I would like to do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and it would be P2709.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Relying on the theory of goose versus gander, I'd like to know where they came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will probably find them on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, these documents were found only during the searches. I will provide Your Honours with the source of this document. And it will be P2709.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. But these seem to me to be extracts from newspapers?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Exactly. So open-source document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, one is definitely a newspaper for sure, which is Glas. 2708 is an extract from Glas, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: 2708 is Serbian Democratic Party Livno Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, okay. What's this? This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, you can disregard this one. I haven't used it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is not being tendered, not being used?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, it hasn't been tendered. And this one, you have the B/C/S version behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but it says 26 January 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At the end, exactly. It's when the article was written. The title is --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: "Holding our three fingers in Drvar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is a part of a newspaper or what is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's a part of a newspaper article. Unfortunately, I have to be -- find out and be more specific about which newspaper it was published in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. 2709. That's 2708. All right. Anything else? We reconvene on Monday. Now, on Monday, we will have to -- we will need to adjust the schedule in a way in which to transpose the break that we usually have at 12.30 to 12.00 so that I attend to the swearing in of a new judge, a new ad litem Judge, who will form part of Trial Chamber II, so I need to be there. So we will break at 12.00, and we will reconvene 25 minutes afterwards, et cetera. So the break will be at 12.00, not 12.30. All right? Good. I don't know which courtroom we're working in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Courtroom II. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can't we change this? See if you can work in some other courtroom, Chuqing. All right. I thank you. Have a nice afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 1st day of December, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
